title: Advanced Documentary Filmmaking

jokes.text: My name is Kevin, or so they tell me.
jokes.setup: Documentary confessional opens with what should be a simple self-introduction.
jokes.punchline: He undermines even the most basic fact of identity — his own name — with casual epistemic doubt.
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open joke. The deadpan delivery of existential uncertainty about one's own name is a strong character-comedy hook. Economy is near-perfect — eight words do enormous work establishing the episode's comedic premise.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My name is Kevin G. Chang. I've suffered from amnesia for several years now.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The worst part? I can't even remember my own name.

jokes.text: But by using a special, shiny glass called a mirror, I've estimated that I'm 15 years old, although I have no way of knowing.
jokes.setup: Kevin describes how he has pieced together basic facts about himself.
jokes.punchline: He calls a mirror 'a special, shiny glass' and his age estimate is comically wrong — a grown man guessing 15.
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: the defamiliarization of a mirror (calling it 'special shiny glass') signals the depth of Kevin's supposed amnesia with elegant wordplay, then the punchline — estimating his age as 15 — is absurd and visually contradicted by the audience seeing a grown man. Strong originality and character-specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have a condition where I lose my memory. It's called... I forget what it's called.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This is a mirror. It's special, shiny glass. I see a handsome young man looking back at me.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'd say he's about 15 years old.

jokes.text: why Changnesia affects the memory but not the ability to make forced puns...
jokes.setup: Dean is building a serious case for Changnesia as a legitimate medical condition.
jokes.punchline: He punctures the gravity mid-sentence by noting the convenient symptom pattern — Changnesia selectively spares Chang's pun-making ability.
jokes.explanation: Sly meta-joke: the Dean is simultaneously selling the Changnesia fraud and inadvertently exposing its absurdity. It also retroactively validates all of Chang's terrible puns from prior seasons as a character-defining trait the show is now riffing on. Very well-constructed embedded irony.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I suffer from a condition where I compulsively make puns and wordplay, often at inappropriate moments, completely oblivious to how much it bothers everyone around me.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's really quite a problem. You might say my humor is... un-CHANG-ed.

jokes.text: Then he became a disgraced student, psychopathic music major, homeless vent dweller, security guard, keytarist, power hungry warlord, and now, Kevin.
jokes.setup: The Dean recounts Chang's history at Greendale as though providing medical context.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates through increasingly absurd career phases — keytarist and power hungry warlord land especially hard — then deflates to 'Kevin.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It functions as a highlight reel of four seasons of Chang's absurd character history, delivered with straight documentary gravitas. 'Keytarist' and 'power hungry warlord' are both perfectly chosen for maximum absurdity, and the final anticlimax — 'and now, Kevin' — lands as the perfect deflation. High quotability and strong rewatch value for fans who know the history.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Chang's been through quite a career journey here. Started as a Spanish teacher, then security guard, then... well, the titles got creative. At one point he was 'Deputy Dean of Discipline,' then 'Campus Security Commander,' and by the end... 'Power Hungry Warlord.'

jokes.text: It's sad to see him like this. Well, it's mixed. He was pretty terrible before.
jokes.setup: Dean begins with performative sympathy about Kevin's condition.
jokes.punchline: Immediately corrects himself — the sadness is 'mixed' because Chang was awful.
jokes.explanation: Clean self-correction joke with good economy. The Dean's inability to maintain false sympathy even on camera is funny and character-consistent. The mid-sentence pivot is the structural strength here.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have a theory about Kevin's condition. You see, most people go crazy, but Kevin went un-crazy. It's reverse psychology, but for sanity. The more insane things happen around him, the saner he becomes. It's a very rare medical condition I just invented.

jokes.text: I'm developing a theory which some find controversial. Perhaps Chang actually used to be Kevin, went crazy, and became Chang. And then, at some point, Chang hit his head, went un-crazy, thereby reverting back to regular old Kevin again. That makes no sense.
jokes.setup: The Dean presents his 'controversial theory' about Kevin/Chang's psychological history with mock-academic gravitas.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate off-camera rebuttal: 'That makes no sense.' Then the Dean blithely says 'Told you it was controversial,' treating a logical fallacy as scientific debate.
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man/absurdist structure. The Dean's theory is genuinely circular nonsense, Jeff's interruption is the audience surrogate, and the Dean's reframe of 'controversial' to dismiss legitimate critique is an excellent character beat. 'Told you it was controversial' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's not how the human body works.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Actually, Dean, the Dean is right. If you consume too much dairy, your bones turn into cheese.

jokes.text: Science tells us hitting his head would only cure him if hitting his head was the original cause.
jokes.setup: The Dean's pseudoscience theory is on the table.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a perfectly logical rebuttal as though it's the devastating truth, which it is — the joke is the contrast between the Dean's nonsense and Jeff's reasonable-sounding but also absurd medical standards.
jokes.explanation: Functional supporting joke. Jeff as the voice of reason is well-deployed, but the joke itself is more explanatory setup for the Dean's callback ('Told you it was controversial') than a standalone laugh. Competent but not remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need this grant money for the school. It's absolutely critical for our survival as an institution.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And, oh, it would also help pay for that documentary someone's been making about me.

jokes.text: so we can continue to fight this terrible disease and hopefully, one day, pay for this documentary.
jokes.setup: Dean is delivering a sincere appeal to the Macguffin Institute for a $40,000 grant to study Changnesia.
jokes.punchline: He adds 'and hopefully, one day, pay for this documentary' — revealing the grant money would fund the very film he's making to get the grant.
jokes.explanation: Nice meta-documentary gag. The circular logic (using grant money to make the documentary that secures the grant money) is handled with good economy. The Dean's blithe self-exposure is very consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: So, what did you think of my grant pitch?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It was great, Dean. Really compelling. By the way, we're gonna need a new camera, better lighting, and a Steadicam.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Abed, that's not feedback on the pitch.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, but it's feedback you needed to hear.

jokes.text: How was that, Abed? That's too beggy? No, that was great. But I could use a new camera, with a smoother zoom.
jokes.setup: Dean finishes his grant appeal speech and asks Abed for feedback on performance.
jokes.punchline: Abed ignores the actual question and uses the moment to request a better camera — treating the Dean's manipulation as an opportunity for his own.
jokes.explanation: Very Abed — his priorities are always filmmaking over human concerns. The redirect from 'was I convincing?' to 'I need better equipment' is a sharp character beat. The Dean's vanity ('get my good side') as a secondary joke adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What the hell, Abed?

jokes.text: This documentary needs to be convincing. This needs to be the hoop dreams of things people care about.
jokes.setup: Dean is rallying the troops for the documentary effort.
jokes.punchline: 'Hoop Dreams of things people care about' — the comparison to the acclaimed social-issue documentary is immediately deflated by 'things people care about,' implying Changnesia does not qualify.
jokes.explanation: Smart pop-culture reference deployed with self-awareness. The Dean is simultaneously praising his own cause and inadvertently admitting it's unworthy of serious documentary treatment. The reference earns its place because it's modified with 'things people care about,' showing craft.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, we need to talk about the glitter. This is craft-store glitter, which means it's like 40% actual glitter and 60% broken dreams and plastic shavings.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: If we're going to do this documentary, we need to do it right. We need professional-grade glitter.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not putting my name on a banner that looks like it was made by someone who shops at a dollar store.

jokes.text: The dean wants a propaganda film, but I intend to explore all sides of this serious issue, including those who don't think it's a serious issue.
jokes.setup: Abed gives his confessional about the documentary's editorial direction.
jokes.punchline: He frames 'skeptics' as a legitimate side to cover journalistically, which inadvertently validates the skeptics' position (that it's not serious).
jokes.explanation: Abed's documentary-nerd persona is perfectly deployed. His detached journalistic framing reveals more than he intends. Good character integration — only Abed would approach his friends' crisis as an editorial balance question.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So I checked with the registrar, and Spanish is completely full.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But if I have a minor heart attack, I can get priority registration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: How many heart attacks do you think I'd need for early enrollment?

jokes.text: You gotta be fucking kidding me. / Got it. Beautiful. All right, let's get one more for safety. Jeff, back to one. Jeff?
jokes.setup: Abed ambushes Jeff on camera to get his reaction to the Changnesia documentary.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's expletive-laden disgust is treated as perfect documentary gold by Abed, who immediately calls for a safety take — treating Jeff like an unwilling subject.
jokes.explanation: Abed's filmmaker detachment turns Jeff's genuine frustration into content. 'Back to one' is the perfect absurdist director-speak applied to real life — classic Abed. The gap between Jeff's emotion and Abed's clinical response is the comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, you've committed fraud, identity theft, impersonation of a security officer, breaking and entering...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You've stolen cars, you've faked your own death, you've terrorized a campus, you've run an illegal gaming operation...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And most egregiously, you consumed your twin brother in the womb.

jokes.text: I'm telling you, we should have sprung for the name brand glitter. Look, cheap glitter, expensive glitter. Money talks, people.
jokes.setup: Study group is making banners for Kevin/Chang.
jokes.punchline: Pierce is passionately arguing about glitter quality as if it's a serious business matter.
jokes.explanation: Decent background character joke. Pierce's pomposity applied to trivial matters is a reliable character beat. 'Money talks, people' as a verdict on glitter is funny but not exceptional — it's mid-tier Pierce content.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Things are bigger when you look through this!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I can see the pores on my skin! I'm disgusting!

jokes.text: The history of ice cream class had another heart attack. Three more, and we're all in. Yes.
jokes.setup: Study group is discussing casual campus news.
jokes.punchline: A student in an elderly-attended class had a heart attack, and Troy (or Britta) is gleefully tracking the death toll as a waiting list strategy.
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark joke with great economy. The casualness of treating classmates' cardiac events as a waitlist lottery system is delightfully morbid. 'Yes.' as the button is perfect deadpan. Gets better the more you think about the implications.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Kevin isn't real. You guys are all crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Kevin is as real as my life in the Kalahari.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, that's the thing — Kevin is definitely not real. But your Kalahari thing, at least that's fiction we all agree on.

jokes.text: Fine. I'll tell him. But one day, you'll all be old and slow and lose at things, and when that day comes, I won't remember what I'm doing now.
jokes.setup: Group hesitates to explain the Macguffin situation to Pierce.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's threat of future indifference undermines itself — he admits he won't remember his own grudge — and is delivered with complete self-unaware pomposity.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce: a threat that collapses under the weight of his own senility. The self-undermining logic is characteristically Chevy Chase-era Pierce. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My business slogan is 'Kevin-ly' — as in, heavenly, but with my husband's name!

jokes.text: He kept the dean in a dungeon. He tried to kill us. He ate his twin in utero.
jokes.setup: Jeff arguing that Chang is dangerous and shouldn't be trusted.
jokes.punchline: The list of genuine grievances escalates to 'ate his twin in utero' — an in-universe claim that is both horrifying and absurdly specific, delivered as a logical argument.
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation joke. The list moves from 'kept dean in dungeon' (bad) to 'tried to kill us' (worse) to 'ate his twin in utero' (preposterous and primal). The in-utero detail is the gem — it references prior Chang lore while being maximally absurd. Good economy and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not calling you Kevin.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Okay, Jeff.

jokes.text: That was Chang. This is Kevin. / They're the same idiot.
jokes.setup: Shirley defends Kevin's separate identity from Chang.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate flat 'They're the same idiot' deflates the philosophical distinction.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'The same idiot' as a philosophical rebuttal to identity theory is funny in its reductiveness. Plays well on the show's meta-awareness that Kevin IS Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You know, I believe in second chances. I gave my ex-husband Andre plenty of them when he was cheating on me.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: So if Chang deserves a second chance, then so does everyone.

jokes.text: Whoa. This makes things smaller. No, no... Bigger. Oh, bigger.
jokes.setup: Kevin is demonstrating childlike wonder — Shirley has just described his innocent perspective.
jokes.punchline: He discovers a magnifying glass (or similar object) and cannot figure out which end enlarges. The comedic beat validates Shirley's description in real time.
jokes.explanation: Good visual-verbal comedy. The joke arrives just as Shirley is praising Kevin's wonder, making it a perfect comedic illustration. Chang's self-delighted 'Oh, bigger.' is a sweet comic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I've been thinking a lot about this, and I realize I may have been too harsh on Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He's a human being with feelings, and we should all try to be more compassionate and understanding.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's why I've decided to sit down with him, hear his side of the story, and then systematically document every insane thing he's done so I can destroy him socially and professionally.

jokes.text: Well, enjoy your collective delusion. I'm going to go get a sandwich, which, unlike Changnesia, is real.
jokes.setup: Jeff is dismissing the group's belief in Kevin.
jokes.punchline: He validates the sandwich's existence as a philosophical contrast to Changnesia — the mundane sandwich is real, the disease is not.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's exit line is sharp and character-appropriate. The philosophical framing ('unlike Changnesia, is real') applied to a sandwich is a good Jeff Winger move — condescending, self-satisfied, and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I know what you're thinking. But here's the thing about my friends - they're incredibly easy to manipulate. I mean, it's almost unfair how gullible they are. Britta believes anything I tell her about psychology. Troy will follow me anywhere if I appeal to his sense of loyalty. Annie does whatever I suggest if I frame it as 'the right thing to do.' And don't even get me started on Abed - he's so busy analyzing narratives that he doesn't see when he's living in one I'm writing. So yeah, maybe I'm not the best friend. But I'm definitely the smartest one in the room. And that's really all that matters.

jokes.text: Jeff, Jeff, Jeff... we want to know how you feel about the Macguffin people visiting. I need it on camera. / It's stupid. / What's stupid? / The whole thing. / Okay, put it together for me. 'The whole thing is stupid.' All right, thanks, buddy. I'll cut it together.
jokes.setup: Abed chases Jeff to get a camera reaction, but Jeff refuses to cooperate.
jokes.punchline: Abed manipulates Jeff's monosyllabic responses into a usable documentary soundbite anyway — 'I'll cut it together' — revealing the constructed nature of documentary filmmaking.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-documentary joke about the manipulation of interview subjects. Abed as documentary filmmaker who will manufacture narrative from resistance is pitch-perfect, and 'I'll cut it together' is a great button exposing the deceptive editorial process. High character integration for Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is very 'Dogme 95' of you.

jokes.text: No, I believe the good lord made Chang Chang. Kevin is a choice.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Shirley if she really believes Chang is Kevin.
jokes.punchline: Shirley reframes Kevin/Chang as a theological/moral question — Kevin is a 'choice,' not a medical condition — which inadvertently echoes certain theological debates about identity in a hilariously misapplied way.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The theological framing ('the good lord made Chang Chang') mixed with the loaded phrasing 'Kevin is a choice' (echoing 'being gay is a choice' rhetoric) is clever, dense, and perfectly Shirley. Only she could deliver this joke — it's theologically framed, moralizing, and weirdly compassionate all at once. Exceptional character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We need to expose Chang for what he really is.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay, but we're gonna need better cameras, lighting rigs, and a steadicam.

jokes.text: Not only have they drunk the Kevin kool-aid, they're in the study room right now, making banners, debating glitter...
jokes.setup: Jeff is venting to Shirley about the group's credulity.
jokes.punchline: 'Debating glitter' as evidence of collective delusion — the mundane detail undercuts the drama of 'drunk the kool-aid.'
jokes.explanation: Callback to the glitter joke that works as a mild laugh. The contrast between apocalyptic rhetoric and craft-supply concerns is funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll host the reception! I've got some great material. You know what they say about women drivers? They're terrible! And what's the deal with airline food? It tastes like airplane! Oh, and here's a good one — I do an impression of an Asian person. *makes offensive accent* 'Hello, welcome to my restaurant!' Classic stuff!

jokes.text: Welcome to Shirley's sandwiches, where the food is Kevin-ly.
jokes.setup: Jeff is lecturing Shirley about helping him stop the Kevin situation; she pivots to greet a customer.
jokes.punchline: The slogan 'Kevin-ly' — a pun on 'heavenly' — reveals she's already incorporated Kevin into her brand, and the pun itself is so terrible it's funny.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural reveal joke. The audience has just been told Shirley doesn't believe in Kevin, then she has 'Kevin-ly' as a branded slogan — exposing either her hypocrisy or her pragmatism. The pun's badness is intentional and lands well. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, partner, first things first. We need detective names.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I was thinking 'The Paperwork Avenger' or something clever with my actual name.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm gonna call you... Reggie.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Reggie? Why Reggie?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I don't know. It just feels like a Reggie.

jokes.text: You hired Chang? / The customers love Kevin. I think it's because he's a good listener. Most words are new to him, so it's all still fascinating.
jokes.setup: Jeff is horrified to discover Chang works at Shirley's sandwiches.
jokes.punchline: Shirley explains Kevin's appeal as a listener: not because he's empathetic, but because language itself is new to him, so he can't tune out.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about the nature of attentiveness. 'Most words are new to him, so it's all still fascinating' reframes incomprehension as a customer service skill. It's also quietly a critique of normal people's inability to listen.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: See, in a detective duo, one guy's gotta be the good cop, and the other guy's gotta be the bad cop.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yes it is.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, it's not.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, I'm a detective. I think I know how detective dynamics work.

jokes.text: Jeff discovers Chang is working at Shirley's Sandwiches — visual reaction beat.
jokes.setup: Jeff came to Shirley as the 'only sane person left' — she's his ally against Chang.
jokes.punchline: He discovers Chang is her employee. The visual of Chang in a sandwich-shop uniform, apparently a beloved customer favorite, is the punchline to Jeff's entire monologue.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structural joke — the last ally turns out to have already defected. The reveal is well-timed and well-staged, though it's a standard structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You think I don't remember? I remember everything. Every single word you said to me about being a lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: [recites entire lengthy conversation word-for-word]

jokes.text: I'm Kevin. And you are? / Not calling you Kevin. / Hi, not calling you Kevin. What are you having? / None of this.
jokes.setup: Kevin introduces himself to Jeff with innocent sincerity.
jokes.punchline: Jeff refuses the name, so Kevin takes 'Not calling you Kevin' as his actual name and greets him as such. Jeff's 'None of this' is both a food order refusal and an existential statement.
jokes.explanation: Excellent rapid-fire joke. Kevin adopting 'Not calling you Kevin' as a greeting is the perfect logic of a person who takes all language literally and freshly. 'Hi, not calling you Kevin' is a perfect absurdist beat. And 'None of this' works on two levels — refusing both the menu and the entire situation. Great economy, strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you remember everything?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Perfect memory. It's a gift.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That must be exhausting.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have a condition. My brain filters out emotional pain.

jokes.text: Like how I gave Andre a second chance. It doesn't mean I forgot. I just forgave. / Chang didn't sleep with a stripper. He tried to kill us. Why does everyone keep forgetting about that?
jokes.setup: Shirley is making a moral equivalence argument between forgiving Andre and forgiving Chang.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's exasperated counter — 'Chang didn't sleep with a stripper, he tried to KILL us' — exposes the profound mismatch in Shirley's moral equivalence.
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke. The escalation from 'sleeping with a stripper' to 'tried to kill us' as a moral comparison is perfectly absurd, and Jeff's exasperation at having to point this out — 'Why does everyone keep forgetting about that?' — is the perfect frustrated-straight-man button. High character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you've been playing me this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm not Chinese, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Yes, you are.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, I'm Korean.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... that's basically the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Is it? Would you like me to explain the difference, or should I just assume you're not interested in learning?

jokes.text: What Shirley said really made me think. I mean, all my friends believe this guy. What does it say about me that I don't? Hmm?
jokes.setup: Jeff's confessional shows apparent genuine reflection.
jokes.punchline: He looks directly at the camera expectantly after 'What does it say about me that I don't?' — as if waiting for someone to validate him. The beat implies he wants reassurance he's right, not actual self-reflection.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Jeff's 'Hmm?' to camera is a performative gesture of self-examination that reveals the opposite. It's consistent with Jeff's character of performing introspection without doing it. The 'Yes?' follow-up adds to the beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I was going to call it 'Docutainment' but apparently that's already a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So I came up with 'Edutainment'... which is also apparently a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Fine. 'Infotainment.' But I invented that one first in my head.

jokes.text: Ugh, and cue wet blanket Winger to tell us that we're all wasting our time. / Actually, no. I had a really good conversation with Shirley, and I realized I've been acting like a jerk.
jokes.setup: Britta anticipates Jeff's predictable killjoy behavior.
jokes.punchline: Jeff subverts expectations with apparent sincerity — but the audience suspects (correctly) it's a manipulation.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup — Britta calling out the trope before it subverts it adds a meta layer. The rewatch value is higher because on rewatch you know Jeff is already plotting. Gets funnier retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So I walk into this bar, right? And there's this guy at the counter...

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I said to him, 'Hey buddy, what's with the long face?' He says, 'My wife left me.'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I said, 'Well, that's what you get for marrying a woman who can think for herself!'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Then I realized—she probably left because of his terrible personality. Like his whole ethnic group's terrible personality.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Which reminds me of this time I paid for a woman's company, but I'm not going to say where because that would be illegal in most states.

jokes.text: And can you say 'powwow' instead of 'conversation'? It just sounds more you.
jokes.setup: Abed is directing Jeff's confessional for the documentary.
jokes.punchline: Abed asks Jeff to use 'powwow' because it sounds 'more him' — Abed is shaping the documentary's characterization of Jeff, and also the word choice is weirdly specific and culturally loaded.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed joke about documentary construction. 'Powwow' as the more authentically 'Jeff' word is odd and funny. The meta point (Abed is literally scripting Jeff's authenticity) is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay Garrett, just keep the camera steady.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I'm trying, but this thing weighs a ton!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's not that heavy. Just hold it up.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Easy for you to say. My arms are already shaking.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We've only been filming for thirty seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Thirty seconds?! It feels like thirty minutes!

jokes.text: It says I have gullible friends who will believe anybody, and I need to make that anybody me. By exposing Chang in front of the whole school.
jokes.setup: Jeff seemed to be having a moment of genuine reflection. He now reveals his true motive.
jokes.punchline: He's not turning over a new leaf — he's just switching from skeptic to manipulator, using the group's gullibility as a tool.
jokes.explanation: Good reveal payoff on the misdirection setup. The logic of 'I need to make that anybody me' is deliciously cynical and very Jeff Winger. The reveal that his 'growth' was strategy is a satisfying twist.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're Sherlock Holmes?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, you're Sherlock Holmes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But I thought—

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're Watson. I'm Holmes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why do you get to be Holmes?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because I'm smarter than you.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not how detective partnerships work!

jokes.text: Wow. Much like the classic documentary Capturing the Friedmans, my story just took a completely unexpected turn.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he's been plotting all along.
jokes.punchline: Abed reacts not with moral judgment but with documentary comparison — framing Jeff's manipulation as a narrative asset. The specific reference to Capturing the Friedmans (a documentary where the filmmaker's complicity is questioned) adds a layer.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-documentary joke. Abed's reference to Capturing the Friedmans is knowing — it's the documentary where the filmmaker's ethics are most in question, making it the perfect analogy. Only Abed would react to real-world manipulation with cinematic gratitude.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: I saw something emerge from that trout tank. Something with eyes full of rage and... purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: The trout. They know what we did to them. They're coming back for revenge.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: Don't you see? This is their endgame. Years of planning in that tank, waiting for the moment we'd least expect it.

jokes.text: Jeff, if you want this done right, I'm going to need a steadicam for Garrett. That's showbiz.
jokes.setup: Abed is on board with Jeff's plan and stating his requirements.
jokes.punchline: 'That's showbiz' — delivered completely deadpan about a steadicam for Garrett, a minor recurring character used as incompetent comic relief.
jokes.explanation: Good economy joke. Abed invoking professional filmmaking standards for a community college documentary involving Garrett is absurd. 'That's showbiz' as a deadpan button on equipment demands is a funny detached Abed move.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, it's just a naked man. For a second there I thought it was a vengeful trout.

jokes.text: And that's why Pierce should host the reception. He speaks their language. / Finally, somebody's making some sense. / I've got a blackface senor Wences bit I've been workshopping. / Perfect.
jokes.setup: Jeff claims Pierce should host the Macguffin reception because he 'speaks their language' (older, wealthy, establishment).
jokes.punchline: Pierce reveals his prepared 'bit' is a blackface Señor Wences impression — and Jeff says 'Perfect,' because he wants the presentation to fail (sabotage). The joke works on two levels: Pierce's oblivious racism and Jeff's cynical approval of it.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered dark comedy. Pierce's racism is played for horror-comedy as a known character trait, but the real joke is Jeff weaponizing it knowingly as a sabotage mechanism. 'Perfect.' landing after 'blackface Señor Wences bit' is a shock-punchline that works because we understand Jeff's ulterior motive. High character integration — this joke requires both Pierce's obliviousness and Jeff's cynicism.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: Look, I don't know anything about the employees at the trout farm. That's not really my world.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: I mean, I got a dog at home, but that's about it.

jokes.text: Annie, we need to find out what happened to Kevin before he showed up at Greendale. What hellish experiences did he overcome during those missing months? Do you think you can use your forensic knowhow to do some investigating? / Investigating? Obvi.
jokes.setup: Jeff assigns Annie a task framed as genuine concern for Kevin.
jokes.punchline: Annie's immediate 'Obvi' is both a character note (her eagerness) and a funny tonal contrast with Jeff's melodramatic framing ('hellish experiences').
jokes.explanation: Light character beat. Annie's perkiness vs. Jeff's manufactured gravitas is reliable but not especially sharp here. 'Obvi' is a dated-sounding affectation that works for Annie's character but doesn't elevate the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Sullivan
dialogue.line: Hey, I run a tight ship here. We treat those trout better than SeaWorld treats their whales.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Sullivan
dialogue.line: Well, okay, I have a dog at home that I... I don't really pay much attention to, but the trout? Those trout are like my children.

jokes.text: 'Investigating? Obvi.'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Annie if she can use her 'forensic knowhow' to investigate Kevin's past.
jokes.punchline: 'Obvi' — Annie's immediate enthusiasm for investigation is so total that she can barely finish the word 'obviously.' Light character note.
jokes.explanation: Light but character-consistent. Annie's enthusiasm for procedural investigation is well-established. 'Obvi' is a small character detail — she's young and eager enough to use the abbreviation. Not a big laugh but a smile moment.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The victim was found in the study. A cup of coffee sat beside him, still warm. Half-drunk. The question wasn't who killed Sullivan—it was why. Why would someone leave a perfectly good cup of coffee? The answer was elementary: because Sullivan was a monster.

jokes.text: Can I help? / If you're willing to learn, sure, partner. / 'Partner.' I like that. / I'm going to call you 'Houlihan.' / 'Partner' and 'Houlihan.' / Okay. / No, we won't.
jokes.setup: Troy wants to join Annie's investigation; Annie offers a patronizing 'partner' nickname.
jokes.punchline: Annie names Troy 'Houlihan' (from MASH) — a hierarchical nickname that Troy immediately accepts with a pleased 'Okay,' followed by them simultaneously agreeing/disagreeing about working it out.
jokes.explanation: Good running setup for the Partner/Houlihan bit to come. The simultaneous 'Yeah, we will' / 'No, we won't' at the end is a crisp character beat — Troy immediately slipping into the buddy-cop dynamic while Annie resists it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm leaving with this evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No you're not. Everything you just said is a lie.

jokes.text: In an investigation, one dude always has to go opposite the other dude. That's how they get things done.
jokes.setup: Troy is explaining to Annie why he's contradicting her in the investigation.
jokes.punchline: Troy has derived investigation methodology entirely from buddy-cop movie tropes — 'one dude always has to go opposite the other dude' is his sincere theory of how detection works.
jokes.explanation: Very Troy. His pop-culture-informed worldview as a sincere life philosophy is one of his defining character traits, and 'one dude always has to go opposite the other dude' is a perfectly absurd distillation of buddy-cop logic. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: Look, I care about these people like they're family. We have dignity, we have respect for one another.

dialogue.speaker: Sullivan
dialogue.line: But yeah, okay, they work 16-hour days for minimum wage and I pocket the difference. But that's business, and we're still friends.

jokes.text: Oh, that's me. / I want you to take this camera and follow Chang around for his day-to-day. Really get into the life of a functioning Changnesiac.
jokes.setup: Jeff addresses Britta and then 'Shirley' — but Shirley wasn't paying attention and responds to 'Shirley' with 'Oh, that's me.'
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, that's me' — implying Shirley is so distracted she needed to be reminded of her own name. Also 'functioning Changnesiac' as a clinical term is funny.
jokes.explanation: Light reactive joke. Shirley's 'Oh, that's me' is a small beat and 'functioning Changnesiac' as a clinical category is a mild absurdist laugh, but neither is particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Mr. Sullivan, we know what you did. We have witnesses.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You might as well confess now.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Sullivan
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I did it! I did it!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, really?

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Sullivan
dialogue.line: But I had a very good reason — the government is listening through our teeth.

jokes.text: No, you didn't. Shirley said it, remember? [Kevin proceeds to recall the entire prior conversation verbatim, word for word]
jokes.setup: Jeff catches Kevin knowing he's a lawyer. Kevin claims he heard it from Shirley.
jokes.punchline: Kevin then recites the entire prior conversation with photographic precision — every word, attribution, and nuance — which is not only exonerating but also devastatingly incriminating about his memory being perfect.
jokes.explanation: Among the best-constructed jokes in the episode. The escalation is both a defensive move (Kevin technically exonerates himself using the actual facts) AND the punchline (his perfect recall proves his memory is fine). Jeff's growing horror as Kevin goes on longer and longer is the sustained comedic payoff. The structure is elegant: the alibi is itself the crime. High marks across craft dimensions — only Chang could deliver this, and the economy of using his own perfect recall as both defense and exposure is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, my parents named me after a dog?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A German Shepherd named Troy that died in 1987.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I was born in 1989. So my parents wanted a son named after a dog that was already dead? And that's not even the worst part — my middle name is Maximilianus, after a parrot that my uncle had. Also dead.

jokes.text: My short term memory has actually improved. My doctor calls it a, um... side effect.
jokes.setup: Jeff notes the irony of Kevin's perfect recall given his supposed amnesia.
jokes.punchline: Kevin acknowledges the contradiction with a perfectly timed pause before 'side effect' — the word hangs there as an obvious cover story.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the recall scene. The pause before 'side effect' is doing enormous work — it's a character performing improvisation, and both the character and the audience know it's bullshit. The confidence with which Chang/Kevin delivers a transparent lie is the joke. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'insufficient'? Human rights abuses aren't enough for me?

jokes.text: Well played, Chang. The chess match has begun. / What... I'm Chinese?
jokes.setup: Jeff acknowledges the manipulation with movie-villain gravitas: 'Well played, Chang. The chess match has begun.'
jokes.punchline: Kevin deflects with 'What... I'm Chinese?' — using his feigned cultural amnesia to deflate Jeff's dramatic moment.
jokes.explanation: Superb comedic beat. Jeff sets up the antagonist confrontation with theatrical relish, and Chang/Kevin completely deflates it by pretending not to understand the word 'Chang' as a name vs. a cultural identity. 'What... I'm Chinese?' is a perfect one-line reversal — it's funny on its face, it maintains Kevin's cover, and it humiliates Jeff's dramatic posturing simultaneously. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: ♪ The itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water spout... ♪

jokes.text: An 'entrepreneu-her,' if you will. / Or maybe a businesswoman? / Okay, fine. Think inside the box.
jokes.setup: Britta is pitching the angle for Shirley's documentary segment: a feminist framing.
jokes.punchline: 'Entrepreneu-her' is a terrible feminist portmanteau that Britta is clearly proud of. Shirley's flat 'Or maybe a businesswoman?' rejects the gendered gimmick. Britta's sarcastic 'Think inside the box' is a great button.
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta joke: her earnest feminist lens applied ham-fistedly to a situation that doesn't need it. 'Entrepreneu-her' is a deliberately bad pun — the joke is that Britta is proud of it. Shirley's pragmatic rejection is perfect. Great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This footage is slower than a Godard film.

jokes.text: Pierce. How's your act coming? Blackface Señor Wences? Mmm-hmm. How do you think it's coming?
jokes.setup: Jeff checks in on Pierce's planned act for the Macguffin reception.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's rhetorical 'How do you think it's coming?' implies it's going terribly, which is the desired outcome for Jeff. The confidence is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the blackface Señor Wences bit. The implication that it's going badly is the joke, and Pierce's pride in the same thing that horrifies everyone else is consistent. Good running character work.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Everyone practices facial expressions in the mirror. It's completely normal.

jokes.text: In the unlikely event I fail to expose Chang, I'm pretty confident Pierce will make sure we don't get a Grant.
jokes.setup: Jeff confessional about his sabotage plan.
jokes.punchline: He calmly describes using Pierce's racism as a backup plan to torpedo the grant application — a coolly cynical acknowledgment delivered with no self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Good dry confessional beat. Jeff's casual framing of Pierce's racism as a contingency plan is a sharp character moment — it shows how thoroughly Jeff has instrumentalized his friends.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hey Kevin, go get me a coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Okay! Right away, sir!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: See? This is what I'm talking about. Respect. Obedience.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm so happy to help!

jokes.text: What you talkin' about, hookey? / Wow, that bit could not get any more perfect. Wait a minute. I haven't introduced you to my Asian wife yet. / Uh-oh... I was wrong.
jokes.setup: Pierce demonstrates his act — which now includes a 'What you talkin' about' reference (Gary Coleman impression) plus introducing an 'Asian wife' puppet/prop.
jokes.punchline: Jeff thought the act had hit peak offensiveness, but it escalates further. 'Uh-oh... I was wrong' is a perfect understated button.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation joke. The structure is: Jeff thought the act was at maximum offensive potential, then it escalates. 'I was wrong' is a perfectly dry callback. The comedic logic of an act that keeps adding racist elements is very Pierce. High structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what we're going to do. We set the trap, we wait for Chang to take the bait, and then—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We spring it on him. The smoking gun we've been looking for.

dialogue.speaker: Chang's Ex-Wife
dialogue.line: I'm ready to tell him everything.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Perfect. This ends today.

jokes.text: This is the place. / No, it's not.
jokes.setup: Annie and Troy arrive at a location for investigation.
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately contradicts Annie's declaration with a flat 'No, it's not' — presumably while looking at the clearly correct location.
jokes.explanation: Callback to Troy's theory that investigators must always contradict each other. It's executed with perfect economy — two words is all the punchline needs. The visual comedy of Troy presumably looking at an obviously correct location adds to the gag.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've been documenting Kevin's phone calls. He doesn't understand doorknobs.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He doesn't understand how keys work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He doesn't understand the concept of 'outside.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And yesterday, he called me asking what a 'phone' is.

jokes.text: What are you, the trout police? Because if you are, you're legally bound to tell me, or else it's entrapment.
jokes.setup: Annie and Troy arrive at a trout farm asking questions.
jokes.punchline: Sullivan immediately invokes 'the trout police' and legal entrapment doctrine — implying trout farming is policed to a degree that requires legal protections.
jokes.explanation: Very funny guest character introduction. The specificity of 'trout police' and the legal paranoia around it is an absurdist character beat that efficiently establishes Sullivan as someone who has thought deeply about trout-crime jurisprudence. 'You're legally bound to tell me' is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I found this phone number written on a napkin, and I thought, 'What if this is my soulmate?' So I called it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Turns out it was a Pizza Hut, but you know what? I found beauty in that random number.

jokes.text: I'm not saying that the trout are a vengeful breed, but if they were, I'd probably be public enemy number one.
jokes.setup: Sullivan explains why he was scared when something emerged from the trout tank.
jokes.punchline: He has apparently spent real time contemplating whether trout would seek revenge on him — and concluded he'd be their primary target. The logic is absurd but internally consistent.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The absurdist logic is airtight — of course a trout farmer would be public enemy number one for vengeful trout. The hedge ('I'm not saying that the trout are a vengeful breed, but if they were') is the structural gem: it both commits to and disclaims the premise simultaneously. The delivery implies Sullivan has genuinely reflected on this. Excellent originality, economy, and earned humor.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Those phone calls were very important to me. I was learning who I was, you know? Finding myself.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: But I realize now, maybe I was just trying to connect with someone. Anyone, really.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Because deep down, I'm still Kevin. Kevin who just wants to be understood.

jokes.text: So the figure that emerged, it was that man? / Yeah, and I was pretty relieved when I found out it was a naked Asian guy, and not an angry trout.
jokes.setup: Annie is pressing Sullivan to confirm the identity of the person who emerged from his trout tank.
jokes.punchline: Sullivan frames 'naked Asian guy' as the relief scenario — the comedic comparison being that an angry trout would have been worse.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The setup of trout revenge anxiety pays off immediately — 'not an angry trout' as the relief phrasing is exactly right. The deadpan of 'naked Asian guy' as the preferable option is excellently constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Kevin, I know what you're doing. You're not actually this nice.

dialogue.speaker: Kevin
dialogue.line: I don't know what you mean, Jeff. I'm just being myself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, no, no. You're manipulating everyone. I can see right through you.

dialogue.speaker: Kevin
dialogue.line: That's a shame. I was hoping we could be friends.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Friends? We can't be friends! You're evil! Look, he's evil, right? Someone back me up here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Fine. Kevin, tell everyone about the time you... you... backstabbed someone. Dramatically.

dialogue.speaker: Kevin
dialogue.line: I've never backstabbed anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because you're too clever! You use psychological manipulation instead!

dialogue.speaker: Kevin
dialogue.line: Or maybe I'm just a good person.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Nobody's just a good person! It's statistically impossible!

jokes.text: Oh, it must have been around June. I remember because my milkweed allergies were acting up something fierce.
jokes.setup: Annie asks when Chang/Kevin appeared at the farm.
jokes.punchline: Sullivan pinpoints the date using milkweed allergies as his mnemonic system — an absurdly specific and mundane life detail offered without irony.
jokes.explanation: Solid character-flavor joke. Sullivan's milkweed allergies as a calendar system is a nice absurdist detail that efficiently characterizes him as someone who lives by rural seasonal rhythms. 'Acting up something fierce' is good color.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've been investigating Chang, and what I found is absolutely insane. This man has been lying about everything.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: His entire romantic history? Completely fabricated. He's been telling people he dated a woman named 'Consuela' for three years.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Turns out? Consuela is his mother's name. He's been role-playing with a cardboard cutout.

jokes.text: Employees? What do I look like, trout world? No employees. Heh, just me. And my dog.
jokes.setup: Annie asks how many employees Sullivan has at his farm.
jokes.punchline: 'What do I look like, trout world?' — a riff on 'Sea World' implying a large corporate trout enterprise. The scale of the insult to his modest farm is funny.
jokes.explanation: Good character specificity. 'Trout world' as the imagined corporate adversary is a nice piece of world-building comedy — Sullivan exists in a world where there's apparently a commercial-scale trout enterprise he disdains. The 'and my dog' addition is a dry beat.

dialogue.speaker: Grant Committee Member
dialogue.line: We've reviewed the evidence of this 'Changnesia' outbreak. Your passionate testimony has convinced us it's a legitimate public health crisis that requires immediate funding.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Wait, what? No, I was having a breakdown. I was trying to prove it's not real!

dialogue.speaker: Grant Committee Member
dialogue.line: Your emotional investment only confirms the severity. We're allocating $2 million to Changnesia research.

jokes.text: A spike in production in June, at the peak of milkweed allergy season? Something on this trout farm was starting to smell... wrong.
jokes.setup: Annie is doing a confessional-style investigative narration, like a true-crime documentary.
jokes.punchline: She's doing a film-noir/documentary investigator voice over milkweed allergies and trout — the genre mismatch (true crime gravitas + trout farm trivia) is the joke. 'Smell... wrong' is a deliberately staged dramatic pause over the mundane.
jokes.explanation: Good genre-parody beat. Annie fully committing to investigative-documentary voice over trout farm trivia is funny. The pun 'smell... wrong' (trout farm, smelling) adds a layer of wordplay. Classic Community meta-genre work.

dialogue.speaker: Macguffin Institute representative
dialogue.line: We've decided to award Greendale the grant. You could say we're really... raising the bar.

jokes.text: Annie and Troy perform the good cop/bad cop bit at the trout farm: Troy is bad cop on command even though Sullivan hasn't admitted to anything yet.
jokes.setup: Annie signals Troy to be 'bad cop' at a seemingly neutral moment in questioning Sullivan.
jokes.punchline: Troy flies into the scripted bad cop role for no investigative reason — the genre performance takes over from actual procedure.
jokes.explanation: A payoff to Troy's earlier meta-observation about investigative genre conventions. Annie and Troy are cosplaying detectives rather than doing detection. The fact that it accidentally WORKS (Sullivan confesses) is a nice ironic resolution.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about my behavior lately, and I realize I've been acting just like Chang. Actually, no—I've been out-Changing Chang. And that's saying something, because Chang is basically Chang.

jokes.text: Partner and Houlihan. / Shut up, Kevin! / Partner and Houlihan. / I don't understand.
jokes.setup: Sullivan has confessed; Chang/Kevin wanders in and identifies them by their nicknames.
jokes.punchline: Kevin calling them 'Partner and Houlihan' — proving he's been paying attention all along — is funny. Sullivan's 'Shut up, Kevin!' reveals he named his dog Kevin.
jokes.explanation: Layered callback payoff. 'Shut up, Kevin!' resolves the dog mystery from earlier (Sullivan mentioned 'just me and my dog') and the callback to the nicknames is timed perfectly. The beat has two simultaneous reveals landing at the same moment, which is structurally impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I may be a lot of things, but I'm not a murderer. Unlike some people.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What are you implying?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not implying anything. I'm just saying that if we're comparing ourselves, that's a pretty big difference.

jokes.text: Because he doesn't know about money. Kevin doesn't know about labor laws, or 40-hour work weeks, or that that dude named him after a dog.
jokes.setup: Troy asks why Kevin would work for free.
jokes.punchline: Annie lists the things Kevin doesn't know (money, labor laws) and then, with perfect escalation timing, adds 'or that that dude named him after a dog.'
jokes.explanation: Great escalation structure. The list moves from systemic ignorance (money, labor law) to the specific personal humiliation (named after a dog). The final item is both the darkest and funniest. The escalation from abstract systems to personal dignity is well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I get it now. I understand what it's like to be Chang. His name is so ridiculous that it's actually worth abandoning your entire identity for.

jokes.text: Growing up, I had a cat named Troy, a bird named Troy, and a hamster named Troy. They were all older than me.
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts to the revelation that Sullivan named his dog Kevin.
jokes.punchline: Troy shares that his parents apparently named all their pets Troy — which raises the disturbing implication about how they named their child.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the best standalone laugh. The setup is the dog/Kevin revelation, but Troy's response is completely unpredictable — he pivots to his own family history, which reveals (without stating) that his parents named him after a pet name tradition. 'They were all older than me' is the perfect button that lands the dark implication. Tremendous economy — this joke does so much with so few words. Strong originality, earned, and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed, I'm sorry. I know I hurt you.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's okay. We're good.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah. Though the lighting in here is very three-point, and your positioning is making this feel like a Terrence Malick film, which is beautiful but structurally unsound for character reconciliation.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I think Kevin's struggle just got a lot sexier, Grant-wise.
jokes.setup: Jeff hears about Kevin being used as unpaid labor.
jokes.punchline: He immediately frames human trafficking as 'sexy' in terms of grant appeal — his cynicism converting genuine suffering into a funding strategy.
jokes.explanation: 'Sexier, Grant-wise' is a great line. The colloquial 'sexier' applied to grant applications is an excellent Jeff Winger register collision — MBA-speak crossed with cynical opportunism. The character specificity is high.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed, every time we try to do something, you turn it into some weird documentary about yourself!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not true. I document everything objectively.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You literally made a documentary about making documentaries. About yourself. Making documentaries.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It was meta.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It was narcissistic!

jokes.text: They were supposed to come back with a smoking gun, and all they found was a little human rights abuse. Which, normally, is terrible.
jokes.setup: Jeff confessional about what the investigation turned up.
jokes.punchline: 'Which, normally, is terrible' — the qualifier is the joke. Jeff's parenthetical acknowledgment that human rights abuse is bad (normally) implies it's currently instrumentally useful.
jokes.explanation: Superb deadpan line. 'Which, normally, is terrible' as a parenthetical about human rights abuse is exactly the register of Jeff Winger's moral flexibility. The economy is excellent — the entire joke is in the qualifier. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Wait, Kevin, I have to know — were you really a reformed man this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Jeff, Jeff, Jeff... did you really think I changed? I was just stringing you along.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: You were... what?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Looks like I really had you on the hook, Winger. Guess you could say I was fishing for your trust.

jokes.text: Do you want it bad enough to rent me a crane? And maybe license an expensive song?
jokes.setup: Jeff demands all footage from Abed.
jokes.punchline: Abed converts Jeff's demand into a negotiation for filmmaking resources — he will give Jeff what he wants in exchange for professional production upgrades.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed joke about filmmaking priorities. His negotiating leverage being equipment rather than any human concern is perfectly in character. The crane and expensive song payoffs come later, making this a setup joke with strong payoff value.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yes! Finally, you understand my master plan! I've orchestrated everything from the shadows, and now—wait, why am I telling you this? This is exactly what the villain does before they lose. I've made a terrible mistake.

jokes.text: unusable crap is generous. It goes on like this for another 12 hours. I couldn't even get through it all, and I sat through The Tree of Life.
jokes.setup: Abed is reviewing Shirley and Britta's documentary footage.
jokes.punchline: He invokes The Tree of Life — a notoriously slow Terrence Malick film — as his benchmark for endurance, and even that film couldn't prepare him for the footage.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The Tree of Life reference is perfect — it's the culturally specific film that film-savvy viewers would recognize as an endurance test for cinema audiences, and using it as a benchmark for twelve hours of Shirley and Britta's singing is very funny. High character integration: Abed would know this reference and deploy it precisely.

jokes.text: When he's alone, he mostly just practices smiling and frowning. We've all done it.
jokes.setup: Jeff spots Kevin doing something suspicious on the footage.
jokes.punchline: Abed deflates the suspicion — Kevin is just practicing basic facial expressions — and then 'We've all done it' normalizes it in a way that makes it weirder.
jokes.explanation: Very good joke. 'We've all done it' as a normalization of practicing emotions in private is both a knowing admission and an absurd generalization. It's also quietly great character comedy for Abed — a person who would practice smiling and frowning analytically. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: And all thanks to Britta. / Don't ruin this.
jokes.setup: Jeff credits Britta for the break in the investigation (accidentally capturing Kevin's phone call).
jokes.punchline: Abed's immediate 'Don't ruin this' — implying Britta's involvement is a taint on any success — is a crisp character insult.
jokes.explanation: Good economy joke. 'Don't ruin this' is a perfect Abed three-word response that says everything about how the group views Britta's competence. It's essentially 'even Britta can't get credit for this.'

jokes.text: You shut up. / But I love you. / You get yourself in the kitchen, and make me a burrito. / Oh, okay, yay! Oh, thank you.
jokes.setup: Pierce is rehearsing his act — a Señor Wences-style routine with a hand/face character.
jokes.punchline: The 'wife' character's dynamic is immediately revealed as abusive — Pierce commands her to make him a burrito; she responds with cheerful compliance — played as a comedy bit that is itself the dark joke about how Pierce views gender dynamics.
jokes.explanation: Pierce performing his own worst instincts through a ventriloquism-style routine is a pointed character joke. The act reveals Pierce's actual worldview — domineering, racialized — which the show is satirizing. High character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin was a victim of human trafficking.
jokes.setup: Jeff's presentation builds dramatically.
jokes.punchline: He announces human trafficking with the gravity of a courtroom revelation — but the audience knows this is being cynically weaponized for grant appeal.
jokes.explanation: Callback payoff on the 'sexy Grant-wise' joke. The human trafficking angle is now being deployed as Jeff promised. The dark irony of genuine human suffering being theatrically announced for grant money is the joke.

jokes.text: So please welcome to the stage the former Mrs. Ben Chang, Alessandra.
jokes.setup: Jeff builds to his big reveal — a person who can jog Kevin's memory.
jokes.punchline: He's brought Chang's ex-wife as a memory trigger — a move that seems sweet but is actually a trap designed to force Chang to either reveal his memory or perform emotional vulnerability publicly.
jokes.explanation: Good structural moment. The reveal of the ex-wife is played as an emotional moment but functions as a chess move. The audience sees both layers simultaneously, which is well-constructed tension.

jokes.text: Oh... You love her so much, you called her over and over and over again, even though you don't know her or how to use a phone or what a number is.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals the phone evidence — that Kevin called the ex-wife's number repeatedly from the vents.
jokes.punchline: He adds 'or how to use a phone or what a number is' — escalating the supposed depth of Kevin's amnesia while simultaneously suggesting miraculous devotion.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The escalating qualifiers — 'even though you don't know her or how to use a phone or what a number is' — are satirizing Jeff's own manipulation. The list gets more absurd with each addition.

jokes.text: Where'd you get the number, Chang? / I found it in the vents! It's 555-0190. And it was the most beautiful thing I'd ever seen.
jokes.setup: Jeff accuses Chang of secretly remembering and reaching out to his ex-wife.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's explanation — he found a phone number on a slip of paper in the vents ('the most beautiful thing I'd ever seen') — is both a plausible Kevin explanation and an absurdly romantic description of a phone number.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny in equal measure. 'The most beautiful thing I'd ever seen' applied to a phone number is touching absurdism. The vent detail connects to Chang's established vent-dwelling history, making it character-specific.

jokes.text: Look, if he doesn't remember her, then this wouldn't bother him. My logic is flawless!
jokes.setup: Jeff is grabbing and shaking Chang/Kevin while the dean and audience react in horror.
jokes.punchline: 'My logic is flawless!' — declared while doing something deeply unhinged, is the perfect Jeff Winger self-justification. His logic is technically correct but socially catastrophic.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's signature lines. 'My logic is flawless!' shouted while shaking an amnesiac in front of an audience is a quintessential Jeff Winger moment — his lawyer brain justifying emotional cruelty. The gap between self-assessment ('flawless') and observable reality (everyone horrified) is the comedy engine. Very quotable, high character integration.

jokes.text: Things got so ugly, I hesitate to even show you this footage. But I will let you see me reacting to it. That'll probably be more than you can handle.
jokes.setup: Abed is narrating the chaotic confrontation scene.
jokes.punchline: He's editorializing his own documentary — deciding to spare the audience the footage but show himself reacting to it, as though his face is the more interesting subject.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-documentary joke. Abed filtering the audience's experience of his own documentary — deciding that his reaction face is 'more than you can handle' — is a perfect parody of self-important documentary filmmaking. The understated confidence ('that'll probably be more than you can handle') is a great deadpan. High originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Mmm... Actually, it's not that bad, but this keeps the story moving.
jokes.setup: Abed reacts to the footage he said would be too much to handle.
jokes.punchline: His actual reaction is mild — 'not that bad' — but he's decided to leave the dramatic framing in because it's narratively useful.
jokes.explanation: Superb callback payoff on the meta-documentary gag. Abed admitting the footage 'isn't that bad' but keeping the narrative framing anyway — 'this keeps the story moving' — is a devastating and funny deconstruction of documentary manipulation. It's also meta-commentary on how Community itself constructs emotional beats. Among the best Abed moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Hey, Alessandra, his last girlfriend was a charred mannequin leg!
jokes.setup: Jeff is continuing his increasingly unhinged confrontation.
jokes.punchline: In desperation, he brings up a charred mannequin leg as Chang's previous romantic interest — an absurd callback to prior Chang lore.
jokes.explanation: Very funny dark escalation joke. Jeff reaching for 'charred mannequin leg' as evidence is a great absurdist image — both specific and maximally strange. The specificity ('charred') elevates it from generic absurdism. Excellent economy and quotability.

jokes.text: Jeffrey, I trusted you and believed in you and fantasized about celebrating over mimosas with you!
jokes.setup: Dean continues condemning Jeff's betrayal.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from 'trusted' and 'believed' (normal) to 'fantasized about celebrating over mimosas with you' — a weirdly specific romantic-adjacent Dean fantasy that has nothing to do with the situation.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton escalation. The pivot from moral condemnation to mimosa fantasies is a perfect character note — his feelings for Jeff are always getting in the way of his judgment. 'Fantasized about celebrating over mimosas with you' is exactly the kind of oddly intimate, non-sexual-but-charged detail that makes the Dean-Jeff dynamic so funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: On behalf of the Macguffin neurological institute, Grant granted.
jokes.setup: The presentation has gone disastrously off the rails — Jeff's confrontation, the charred mannequin leg, the shaking — and everyone expects the grant to be denied.
jokes.punchline: The Macguffin rep grants the grant anyway — because Jeff's meltdown demonstrated exactly the kind of uphill battle Changnesia causes. The plan backfired perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The irony that Jeff's sabotage became the most compelling evidence for Changnesia's impact is a satisfying structural twist. 'Grant granted' is clean and final. The comedic logic is airtight — chaos equals proof of disease legitimacy. High structure score.

jokes.text: So... I guess I did help. Just not in the way I wanted to. But, on the bright side, this is the most well-documented failure of my life.
jokes.setup: Jeff's confessional after his plan backfired.
jokes.punchline: 'The most well-documented failure of my life' — reframing total humiliation through the lens of documentary production quality.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-documentary button on the Jeff storyline. The conceit of framing personal failure through production quality ('well-documented') is a sharp Jeff joke that ties back to the episode's documentary conceit.

jokes.text: By trying to make Kevin a pariah, I accidentally became more Chang than Chang at his Changiest. / That's funny. / Well, I didn't try to kill anyone. / Which no one seems to care about.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Kevin have a reflective moment after the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Jeff makes a self-aware analogy comparing himself to Chang; Kevin responds with 'That's funny' (sincerely appreciating the wit); then adds 'Well, I didn't try to kill anyone' as the actual distinction; then 'Which no one seems to care about' — a callback to Jeff's earlier repeated complaint.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layer joke. 'More Chang than Chang at his Changiest' is a great turn of phrase. Kevin's sincere 'That's funny' as a reaction is itself funny. But the best beat is 'Which no one seems to care about' — a callback to Jeff's earlier repeated frustration that Chang tried to kill people, now delivered by Chang himself. It's a perfect full-circle moment.

jokes.text: Changnesia's hard to understand. At least, that's what people tell me. Now, I don't know a thing about it, which apparently is one of the symptoms, and it's so frustrating.
jokes.setup: Kevin is explaining his condition to Jeff with apparent sincerity.
jokes.punchline: He invokes not knowing about Changnesia as a symptom of Changnesia — a perfectly circular self-defense.
jokes.explanation: Great circular logic joke. 'I don't know a thing about it, which apparently is one of the symptoms' is Catch-22 logic deployed with perfect deadpan sincerity. It's the ultimate unfalsifiable alibi, and Kevin either genuinely believes it or is brilliantly playing it. The ambiguity is the joke. Very Kevin/Chang, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Hi. / My name's Kevin. / I'm not saying I believe him. But I have got an idea of what it feels like to be Chang. Wanting to leave that name behind is the sanest decision anyone can make.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Kevin have a sincere reconciliation moment.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confessional pivot — he won't say he believes Kevin, but he understands the desire to rebrand — frames his own history of self-reinvention as analogous to Changnesia.
jokes.explanation: Good thematic comedic beat. Jeff identifying with Chang's desire for identity reinvention is both a character insight and a quietly funny self-awareness — Jeff knows he's also performed a persona. 'Wanting to leave that name behind is the sanest decision anyone can make' is sharp.

jokes.text: What the heck, Abed? You knew what Jeffrey was planning to do the whole time? Why can't you ever make a documentary about the thing you plan to make a documentary about? / Don't censor him! / Censorship.
jokes.setup: The documentary screening reveals Abed knew Jeff was plotting.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'Don't censor him!' and Britta's single-word echo 'Censorship.' — Britta reducing a complex issue to one dramatic word — is the classic Britta over-simplification gag.
jokes.explanation: Good Britta joke with great economy. 'Censorship.' as a one-word political declaration is a perfect Britta beat — she hears 'censor' and deploys her go-to issue without context. Troy's earnest escalation sets it up well.

jokes.text: This is the documentary. / Ugh. / Abed, you gotta teach me how to use that camera.
jokes.setup: Dean complains that the documentary became something other than what he planned.
jokes.punchline: Abed's simple 'This is the documentary' is a filmmaker's declaration that the unplanned story is the real one. Pierce immediately pivots to wanting camera skills — missing the point entirely.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-documentary coda. Abed's declarative 'This is the documentary' is a thematic statement that also lands as comedy. Pierce's immediately self-interested pivot undercuts the gravity well.

jokes.text: Guys... I'm sorry. I really screwed up. I hope you can forgive me. / Already forgotten. / Oh... / Kevin... / What are we laughing about? / Oh, Kevin. / Kevin... / Adorable. / Good job. / I don't get it.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a sincere apology to the group.
jokes.punchline: Kevin responds with 'Already forgotten' — a perfect amnesia pun/response that the audience and characters recognize simultaneously. The group's warm laughter at Kevin's perfect inadvertent pun, followed by Kevin's 'I don't get it,' is the topper.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and arguably one of the best single-beat gags in the series. 'Already forgotten' works on three simultaneous levels: (1) it's the literally appropriate response from an amnesiac, (2) it's the perfect sentimental reply to an apology, and (3) it's a devastating pun. The group's knowing laughter followed by Kevin's genuine 'I don't get it' is the perfect button — he inadvertently made the best joke of his life and doesn't know it. Near-perfect structure, economy, and character integration.

jokes.text: Hi, it's me. They all finally bought it. Hook, line, and Winger. I patiently await your further instructions. Chang out.
jokes.setup: The episode appears to have ended sweetly. Chang/Kevin is alone and makes a phone call.
jokes.punchline: 'Hook, line, and Winger' — a pun on 'hook, line, and sinker' using Jeff's surname, confirming the entire thing was a con. The tag scene recontextualizes the entire episode.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional episode-ending joke. 'Hook, line, and Winger' is a perfect wordplay pun that's also a structural reveal — the entire episode was a con. It's maximally efficient: three words confirm the twist, land the pun, and give Chang a villain button line. The final 'Chang out' as a sign-off is an excellent character beat. Among the most satisfying closers the show delivers.

jokes.text: Why did I do that? Man...
jokes.setup: Chang has just dramatically announced himself as a villain to his mysterious caller.
jokes.punchline: He immediately regrets the theatrics — breaking his own cool villain moment with self-conscious embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag on the tag. After the episode's most theatrically satisfying villain moment, Chang immediately deflates it with 'Why did I do that? Man...' — a self-aware cringe that acknowledges he got carried away with his own con. The economy is exceptional; it's almost entirely silent comedy with two lines. Great character beat that keeps Chang from being a straight villain.

tmdb_overview: Greendale comes together to get to the bottom of Chang's amnesia, which Abed films as a documentary. Jeff, however, suspects Chang is faking it.
insight: Meta-comedy reaches peak density with 60 jokes in 60 minutes, mostly character-driven escalations.
